channel.title: HumanAIBrief · 人-AI 行为
channel.description: 人与 AI、机器人及算法系统交互中的信任、采纳、依赖、归因与决策行为研究

item.title: Symmetrical and asymmetrical insights into student adoption of AI-enhanced digital educational systems
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Based on the stimulus–organism–response (SOR) model and the technology acceptance model (TAM), this study investigates how the functional and experiential features of artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced educational systems influence users’ behavioral intention through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. Methods A multi-method approach integrating partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), artificial neural networks (ANN) and necessary condition analysis (NCA) was employed. Results The results of the PLS-SEM analysis indicate that both perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use have a significant positive impact on behavioral intention, with perceived ease of use exerting the strongest effect. Furthermore, the effects of functional and experiential features on perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are asymmetric. ANN analysis confirms the robustness of the findings and identifies perceived ease of use as the most influential determinant of behavioral intention. In contrast, the NCA analysis indicates that perceived usefulness is the only statistically significant necessary condition for achieving higher levels of behavioral intention. Although this necessary relationship is statistically significant, its effect size is small, suggesting that its actual constraining effect is relatively limited. The bottleneck analysis further reveals the constraining characteristics of different stages in the formation of behavioral intention. Discussion By integrating symmetric, asymmetric and necessity-based analytical perspectives, this study provides a more comprehensive understanding of user acceptance behavior in AI-enhanced educational environments.

item.title: Beyond technology acceptance: students’ perceptions and prompt engineering competence in higher education
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into Higher Education requires understanding students' perceptions and competence in interacting with these technologies. This mixed-methods study examined perceptions of GenAI and documented prompt engineering competence in academic tasks among 89 Psychology and Biomedical Engineering students. Study 1 employed a 2 × 2 quasi-experimental factorial design comparing disciplinary area and instructional approach (guided vs. autonomous), complemented by thematic analysis. Students reported favourable views of GenAI, particularly for understanding, learning, guidance, and work planning, while emphasising the need to verify AI-generated information and improve reliability and contextual accuracy. No significant multivariate effects of disciplinary area, instructional approach, or their interaction were found. However, item-level analyses identified two items with higher scores under autonomous instruction after multiple-comparison adjustment. Study 2 examined documented prompt engineering competence in 24 group reports using five rubric dimensions and the exploratory Prompt Competence Index (PCI). No differences between instructional approaches remained significant after multiple-comparison adjustment, although descriptive differences in Iteration and PCI emerged among biomedical engineering reports. Overall, findings support contextualised, iterative, and critically supervised human–AI interaction, while suggesting that instructional differences are context- and indicator-specific. Further validation of the PCI in larger, diverse, and balanced samples is required.

item.title: Participatory design in human-robot interaction research: a systematic review
item.description:
Human-Computer Interaction
Participatory Design (PD) approaches for robot design offer promising avenues for enhancing technological innovation and aligning Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) systems with user needs. Despite their potential, there is a lack of a comprehensive overview of how these approaches have been utilized within the field of HRI. This article presents a systematic review of the literature on how PD is applied in the design of HRI systems, highlighting its advantages and challenges. Data were collected by reviewing 102 selected articles published from 2008 to 2024 in leading scientific databases for robotics. We summarize and classify the selected PD studies based on stakeholder participation, methods, and outcomes, among other aspects. We also report on the contributions of PD methodologies to key HRI issues, including ethical challenges, robot autonomy, and human-robot conflicts. Findings show a growing number of HRI researchers using PD approaches, particularly in the context of social robots for healthcare and assistive services. However, we also found that a perspective where robots are considered the solution to every problem, without fully understanding the realities of the target community, is still prevalent and that some aspects of PD, such as equalizing power relations, situated-based action, and long-term stakeholder engagement, are often overlooked.

item.title: University students’ overreliance on generative AI feedback in the learning process: the effects of perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and metacognitive monitoring
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has introduced an important question in education, when AI provides immediate and reliable feedback, do students use it as a learning support tool or gradually rely on it as a substitute for their own cognitive efforts? Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Offloading Theory, and Metacognitive Monitoring Theory, this study develops a theoretical model to explain the formation process of undergraduate students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Specifically, this study examines the relationships among perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and overreliance on GAI feedback, while further exploring how metacognitive monitoring levels shape this process. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 600 undergraduate students, and structural equation modeling was performed using AMOS 31.0. The results showed that perceived cognitive load significantly and positively predicted cognitive offloading, which further contributed to students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Meanwhile, perceived cognitive load also directly predicted overreliance on GAI feedback. Bootstrap analysis further confirmed that cognitive offloading mediated the relationship between perceived cognitive load and overreliance on GAI feedback. In addition, this study established separate structural equation models for students with different levels of metacognitive monitoring and found distinct patterns in the formation of GAI feedback overreliance. Specifically, students with lower metacognitive monitoring were more likely to be influenced by cognitive pressure during learning, showing a more prominent direct relationship between perceived cognitive load and GAI feedback overreliance. This finding suggests that these students tend to rely more directly on GAI feedback when facing higher cognitive demands. In contrast, students with higher metacognitive monitoring demonstrated a more evident cognitive regulation process, in which cognitive offloading played a more important role in linking perceived cognitive load with GAI feedback overreliance. This indicates that these students may actively adjust their cognitive resource allocation when using GAI, although continuous cognitive offloading may still increase their dependence on AI-generated feedback.

item.title: Dual manipulation of individuals by non-invasive intelligent technologies and its risk governance: from the perspective of the Destiny Machine metaphor
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction The “Destiny Machine” metaphor reveals an ethical concern: big data and artificial intelligence, operating as a data-power social machine, manipulate individuals with pre-determinacy as the core logic. At cognitive-information and behavioral decision-option levels, this manipulation appears as cognitive manipulation by recommendation algorithms and decision-making manipulation by automated decision systems. To uncover its psychological mechanisms and ethical risks, this paper builds a framework integrating ethics and psychology. Methods The Destiny Machine is transformed into an analytical tool with three dimensions: pre-determinacy, irresistibility, and concealment. Drawing on dual-process theory, automation bias, moral disengagement, and psychological reactance, it analyzes how non-invasive intelligent technologies psychologically manipulate individuals and shape their ethical risks, adopting the human-centered approach as the guiding principle for governance. Results Cognitive manipulation by recommender systems, typified by TikTok, leaves users unaware that their cognitive preferences are being systematically reshaped, keeping them imperceptibly immersed. Algorithms achieve this by activating Type 1 processing while bypassing Type 2 scrutiny, confining information to relevance channels, and exploiting automation bias and complacency to lower cognitive vigilance and suppress psychological reactance. Indulging in information cocoons widens users’ cognitive distance from the lifeworld, dissolving their moral attributes as ethical beings. Decision-making manipulation by automated decision systems is most evident in autonomous vehicles’ trolley-problem dilemmas, where passengers’ lives are reduced to quantifiable weights. The system pre-sets decision rules and allows remote intervention at the design end; opaque decision-making subjects and logic, millisecond-level deadlines, and impossibility of exit jointly pre-lock passengers’ fate before the accident occurs. It likewise exploits cognitive processing traits and automation bias, while dispersed agency makes responsibility attribution—and thus psychological reactance—difficult. Pre-coding an individual’s fate at the behavioral decision-option level may deconstruct their meaning world. Discussion Under the Destiny Machine metaphor, such manipulation erodes not only individuals’ autonomy but also their responsibility as moral subjects. Guided by the human-centered approach, it proposes governance schemes with clear actors, sound measures, and reliable benchmarks: a cognitive immune system of transparency and empowerment for cognitive manipulation, and a human-machine collaborative scheme of accountability and remedy for decision-making manipulation, rebuilding passengers’ trust to help them escape.

item.title: Generative AI-assisted self-visualization and self-concept clarity: evidence consistent with a cognitive-mirroring mechanism in human–AI interaction
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now lets people turn verbal self-descriptions into visual self-representations, creating a new setting for studying self-concept clarity (SCC) in human–AI interaction. We tested whether generative AI-assisted self-visualization (GAISV) was associated with higher short-term SCC through cognitive mirroring rather than through general immersive flow, and whether this depends on how far participants identify with the generated image. We introduce the AI Mirror Self-Integration Model and evaluated it in two stages. A pilot study (124 valid participants) examined the Cognitive Mirroring in Human-AI Self-Visualization Scale (CM-HAIS) and supported its use as a task-state measure of reflective self-processing. A randomized main experiment then recruited 328 valid participants. Primary analyses compared three conditions—GAISV, active non-self image generation, and passive image viewing ( N = 246)—with SCC measured immediately after the task and again 48–72 h later (T2 N = 216). A self-description-only condition was retained as an exploratory comparison and was not part of the primary tests. GAISV produced higher post-task and follow-up SCC than both control conditions. In parallel mediation models, the GAISV effect was primarily associated with cognitive mirroring rather than with flow, and the cognitive-mirroring indirect path was stronger than the flow path immediately after the task. Image self-identification was associated with the strength of the cognitive-mirroring path at the post-task assessment, as indicated by the index of moderated mediation; the follow-up moderation evidence was weaker. AI-generated self-images were therefore not clarifying by default. GAISV was associated with higher short-term SCC primarily when the image was experienced as personally identifying and engaged reflective cognitive mirroring rather than mere immersion. Condition differences were statistically reliable but small (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.21–0.27), and the mediation results are mechanism-consistent associations rather than evidence of causal ordering.

item.title: Critical thinking dispositions and perceived support-dependence discrepancy in GenAI-assisted learning: evidence from human–AI interaction pathways
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support academic performance while also creating a perceived gap between AI-supported task completion and independently available competence. This study examined how multidimensional critical thinking dispositions are associated with cognitive offloading, cognitive enhancement, and perceived support-dependence discrepancy (PSD) in GenAI-assisted learning. Methods A cross-sectional survey was administered through Wenjuanxing from March 15 to May 20, 2026, using stratified purposive sampling across six Chinese universities. Of 990 submitted questionnaires, 797 eligible and complete responses were retained. The hypothesized pathways were tested using structural equation modeling, with a separate observed-score moderation analysis for academic stress and additional robustness and measurement-model assessments. Results Inquisitiveness was positively associated with cognitive enhancement (β = 0.515, p < 0.001) and cognitive offloading (β = 0.270, p < 0.001). Open-mindedness (β = 0.091, p = 0.039) and systematicity (β = 0.096, p = 0.029) showed small positive associations with cognitive enhancement, whereas analyticity and truth-seeking were not significantly associated with either interaction pathway. Cognitive offloading (β = 0.448, p < 0.001) and cognitive enhancement (β = 0.207, p < 0.001) were positively associated with PSD. The Academic Stress × Cognitive Offloading interaction was not significant (β = 0.048, p = 0.123; delta R-squared = 0.002). Alternative CFA specifications, a common-method-factor analysis, and reliability sensitivity analyses yielded broadly consistent focal conclusions, while the HTMT assessment provided qualified evidence of discriminant validity. Conclusion Critical thinking dispositions showed heterogeneous associations with GenAI interaction pathways, and both offloading and enhancement were associated with perceived support-dependent competence gaps. Because the outcome was measured with a single self-report item and the design was cross-sectional, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than objectively verified overconfidence, calibration bias, or causal effects.

item.title: Design Principles and Measurement Frameworks for Human-Centered AI and Human-AI Interaction: A Systematic Review
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) are increasingly important as AI adoption expands across high-stakes domains. However, empirical evidence remains fragmented across disciplines, limiting the development of transferable design guidance. This systematic review synthesized empirical research on HCAI and HAX and was reported in accordance with PRISMA guidance. Eight databases were searched, and additional preprint records were identified through arXiv. These searches yielded 9,718 records, of which 44 articles were included in the final review. Findings were organized around three dimensions: outcome metrics, collaboration frameworks and AI roles, and domain-specific patterns. Across studies, AI support was often associated with improved objective task performance, including accuracy, task completion time, and decision quality. Subjective outcomes such as trust, satisfaction, usability, and workload varied with transparency, explanation format, cognitive demand, and perceived control. Results suggest that HCAI and HAX frameworks should support task performance while preserving human autonomy and manageable workload. They should also support appropriate trust and reflect domain-specific needs.

item.title: The impact of AI hallucination on the chatbot service quality in e-commerce: the moderating role of human agent based service recovery
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence has been widely adopted in e-commerce, demonstrating significant advantages in enhancing information processing efficiency and human-computer interaction. However, its inherent hallucination characteristic often results in the generation of false or misleading content that does not align with reality. In e-commerce, such AI hallucination is likely to trigger a crisis of trust among users and lead to negative evaluations of service quality. Clarifying the mechanisms through which AI hallucination affects chatbot service quality and exploring effective strategies to mitigate its negative effects have become critical issues. The study conducted two scenario-based experiments using a scripted chatbot with pre-written responses. No large language model (LLM) generated the experimental responses. Both experiments employed a 2 × 2 between-subjects design to examine the effects of simulated hallucination level and human agent-based service recovery on perceived service quality. Study 1 included 236 participants (129 female and 107 male, mean age = 30.10, SD = 6.76), and Study 2 included 364 participants (172 female and 192 male, mean age = 33.98, SD = 9.81). Mediation effect analysis supported indirect associations between higher perceived AI hallucination and lower perceived chatbot service quality through cognitive dissonance and technical frustration. The moderation effect further indicated that a human agent based service recovery strategy effectively mitigates technical frustration but struggles to reverse cognitive dissonance. This work extends research on AI hallucination in e-commerce and offers practical guidance for platforms on integrating human-AI collaboration to mitigate technological limitations.

item.title: Bridging Human–AI Interaction and Human–Robot Interaction: Shared Challenges, Converging Futures
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
This panel examines the growing convergence of human–AI interaction (HAI) and human–robot interaction (HRI) as intelligent systems become more autonomous, embodied, and embedded in everyday settings such as healthcare, education, homes, and workplaces. Although HAI and HRI have evolved as distinct fields, the panel argues that shared human factors concerns—such as trust, safety, autonomy, teamwork, situation awareness, evaluation, and responsible deployment—now require greater integration across both domains. Drawing on perspectives from leading researchers and doctoral students, the session explores how embodiment, motion, social cues, and system transparency shape human interaction with AI and robots. It also addresses methodological tensions, including laboratory versus field evaluation and short-term versus longitudinal study, while highlighting implications for ethics, training, and design. Overall, the panel aims to identify common challenges, foster cross-disciplinary collaboration, and outline a research roadmap for human-centered intelligent systems that improve performance, well-being, and quality of life across diverse contexts and sectors.

item.title: Changes in Perceptions of Trust in Human-AI Interactions
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
This study examined how educational briefings about Artificial Intelligence (AI) hallucinations influence user trust, caution, and willingness to continue using AI systems. We recruited 51 participants through the online platform Prolific for an online questionnaire evaluating AI use and task-focused AI scenarios. After questions about trust and AI, participants read about common inaccuracies in Large Language Models. Participants showed a significant decrease in self-reported trust, indicating increased awareness of AI limitations. Contrary to expectations, perceptions of AI reliability and competence did not predict willingness to reuse AI in academic scenarios. Affective trust played a stronger role than cognitive trust, with perceived emotional support significantly predicting forgiveness of AI errors. Increased caution also predicted greater recalibration of trust, although willingness to continue using AI remained high. These findings suggest that educational interventions can promote calibrated trust in AI without discouraging continued use, highlighting the importance of transparency and context-sensitive design.

item.title: Semantically enhanced eye-tracking controls in human-robot interaction: a comparison study
item.description:
Ergonomics
Operators controlling robotic systems for sequential manipulation tasks present cognitive loads that vary with how they specify intent to the robot. Limited evidence exists on how semantically mediated voice and gaze interfaces differ in operator performance, visual attention, and perceived workload. This study presents findings of a within-subjects experiment (N = 30) with three control modalities (hand gesture, voice, and eye-tracking). Eye-tracking produced shorter, more consistent completion times (M = 17.10 s, SD = 3.95), indicating stable and efficient performance. Voice Control was associated with more structured but variable action ordering and higher NASA-TLX Mental Demand and Effort scores, consistent with demands from spatial-to-verbal intention translation. Gaze metrics indicated distinct attentional strategies: eye-tracking showed lower spatial entropy and fewer fixations, while voice control exhibited broader workspace scanning. These findings suggest an association between attention-control channel coupling and cognitive resource allocation in semantically enhanced human-robot interaction, informing ergonomic hands-free interface design.

item.title: Beyond trustworthiness: Psychological and institutional drivers of university students' AI chatbot adoption in Vietnam
item.description:
Acta Psychologica
Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in higher education, but it remains unclear whether factors associated with perceived trustworthiness are also associated with students' intentions to adopt them. Drawing on an extended UTAUT2 framework, this study examines how chatbot-specific attributes are associated with trustworthiness, performance expectancy, and hedonic motivation, and how these appraisals, together with UTAUT2 factors, relate to behavioral intention. Survey data from 604 university students in Vietnam were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that ethics (β = 0.294, p < .001) and design (β = 0.458, p < .001) were positively associated with perceived trustworthiness, while social influence was not. Design and interactivity were positively associated with performance expectancy and hedonic motivation. However, perceived trustworthiness (β = 0.043, p = .153), hedonic motivation, and effort expectancy were not significantly associated with behavioral intention. Instead, behavioral intention was most strongly associated with price value (β = 0.408, p < .001), performance expectancy (β = 0.281, p < .001), social influence, and facilitating conditions, and was strongly associated with students' self-reported continued-use tendency (β = 0.754, p < .001). Perceived trustworthiness was not independently associated with behavioral intention in the present model, whereas price value and performance expectancy showed the largest positive associations with intention. This pattern highlights the value of considering trustworthiness alongside instrumental, social, and institutional evaluations when explaining AI-chatbot adoption. The study extends UTAUT2 by integrating these adoption evaluations with an assurance-oriented appraisal of the AI system.

item.title: Ethical for Whom: A Systematic Literature Review of Multicultural Perspectives on Responsible AI Values for the Global Majority
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Responsible AI principles like fairness, accountability, and transparency are built on Western institutional assumptions yet exported as universal standards. We systematically reviewed (N=41) studies from underrepresented regions to identify locally prioritized values and their tensions with dominant discourse. Three frictions emerged: epistemic (whose knowledge counts as ethical expertise), contextual (whether abstract principles survive local conditions), and infrastructural (how resource asymmetries constrain value realization). Our findings show Global Majority scholarship does not simply add new values to the list. They reconfigure ethics through lived experience by redefining the core logic: fairness shifts from individual parity to collective well-being; transparency shifts from technical disclosure to relational trust but bounded by protocol and custom; and accountability shifts from top-down audit to distributed responsibility shaped by labor conditions and data sovereignty. This study advocates for centering epistemic pluralism as a prerequisite for ethically legitimate AI governance rather than treating these frictions as implementation failures.

item.title: Student Engagement and Trust Calibration With Generative AI in a 5S Safety Assessment
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Generative AI is increasingly used in engineering and technology education, but its role in safety education remains underexplored. This study examined undergraduate students’ ( N = 14) human-AI interaction during a 5S workplace safety assessment in a Human Factors course. Using a mixed-methods design, we analyzed User Engagement Scale–Short Form (UES-SF) responses and qualitative reflections after students independently completed a hazard identification task and compared findings with a parallel AI-generated assessment (ChatGPT-4o). Results revealed high perceived reward and value, minimal usability barriers, and mixed focused attention, suggesting task engagement without deep immersion. Qualitatively, students described AI as expanding hazard awareness, improving analytical structure, and accelerating information retrieval, while consistently emphasizing the necessity of human oversight and cautioning against overreliance. Integrated findings position generative AI as a human-in-the-loop decision-support tool: effective for scaffolding systematic reasoning and broadening hazard recognition, but insufficient as a substitute for domain-informed judgment.

item.title: Understanding User Expectations Across Communication Modalities in Human-Robot Interaction: An Elicitation Study
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Human-robot communication is essential to effective human-robot interaction. One way to improve this communication is to design systems that align with users’ mental models and expectations about how robots should convey information. However, little research has examined these expectations across robot morphologies (mobile robot, humanoid robot, manipulator, drone) and behaviors (“Navigation Intention,” “Operating State,” “Affect,” “Target Identification,” “Interaction Intention”). This work addresses that gap through an elicitation study investigating users’ expected communication modalities for human-robot communication. Auditory communication was the most expected modality on average by participants across all scenarios (74.4%), closely followed by visual communication (69.8%), with tactile communication coming in at a distant third (16.3%). However, the dominant expected communication modality in any given scenario varied depending on the morphology and behavior included. Additional analysis highlights the plausibility that these expectations are driven more by behavior than by morphology. These findings can be leveraged to inform the design of future communication strategies and facilitate more effective human-robot interactions.

item.title: If it doesn’t have a soul, it doesn’t hurt? The effect of bullying and social anxiety on the use of conversational AI
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) increasingly functions as a social interaction partner, raising questions about how established interpersonal behaviors transfer to human-AI interaction. The present study examined whether bullying-like behavior directed toward CAI reflects the extension of real world social strategies, and how social anxiety, prior bullying experiences, and AI self-competency contribute to such behavior. Methods Participants ( N = 289) completed measures of social anxiety, prior bullying perpetration and victimization, AI self-competency, and bullying-like behavior directed toward conversational AI. Results Through several analyses, bully-victims exhibited the highest levels of AI-directed bullying-like behavior. The interaction between bullying perpetration and victimization emerged as the strongest predictor in our regression analysis, while prior bullying perpetration alone was not sufficient to explain AI-directed aggression, and prior victimization alone was negatively associated with AI-directed bullying-like behavior. Social anxiety did not directly predict bullying-like behavior toward AI; however, mediation analyses showed that prior victimization fully mediated the relationship between social anxiety and bullying-like behavior towards CAI. Individuals with higher social anxiety were more likely to report victimization, which in turn was associated with increased bullying-like behavior toward AI. AI self-competency did not emerge as an independent predictor. Discussion These findings suggest that AI-directed bullying-like behavior is best understood as a context-dependent behavior arising from the co-occurrence of aggression and vulnerability, rather than a direct extension of general aggressive tendencies. Conversational AI constitutes a distinct relational context that can both reflect and reinforce existing behavioral patterns. This has important implications for understanding how human-AI interactions may shape social behavior and psychological functioning over time.

item.title: Reflections and Recommendations on AI Adoption Practice from a Mixed-Ability Research Group
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Generative AI tools have recently been rapidly adopted by academics in mixed-ability research teams for both personal and professional tasks. While previous work on adoption of AI-based workflows has focused on collaboration and productivity, the perceptions of AI use within research teams remains divided. Through qualitative analysis of interviews of the five members of our mixed-ability research team, we discuss the motivations, challenges, and practices surrounding the use of generative AI in our lab. We reflect on experiences that shaped recommendations for balanced AI use that enable mixed-ability team workflows: (1) managing disability tax & crip time, (2) homogenizing identity, (3) risk disclosure of private information, (4) self-experimentation and miscellaneous tasks, and (5) information seeking. We build upon these themes to present AI practice recommendations we established for our lab to promote AI workflow adoption while preserving agency and disability identity.

item.title: Safe and Accessible AI for Youth with Disabilities and Neurodivergence
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Generative AI systems are increasingly woven into young people’s everyday lives, shaping how they learn, communicate, create, seek support, and understand themselves. For youth with disabilities and neurodivergence, these systems may offer meaningful opportunities for communication support, low-pressure social interaction, personalized learning, and self-expression. However, these benefits are closely tied to new and uneven risks. AI systems may misunderstand disabled and neurodivergent users, reproduce stereotypes, encourage emotional overreliance, or rely on safeguards that are inaccessible, privacy-invasive, and overly surveillant. These concerns sit at the intersection of accessibility, youth digital safety, usable security and privacy, and AI ethics, yet they are rarely studied together. This gap matters because inaccessible or poorly designed safeguards can themselves become sources of harm. In this half-day virtual workshop, we invite researchers, practitioners, designers, educators, advocates, and youth to examine what safe and accessible AI should mean for youth with disabilities and neurodivergence. Through shared discussion and collaborative activities, the workshop will identify key risks, design tensions, and methodological challenges, while beginning to build a shared research and design agenda for this emerging area.

item.title: Learning Python as a Blind Programmer in an AI-Mediated Environment: An Autoethnographic Study
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Programming education is increasingly mediated by AI tools, yet little is known about how blind learners—particularly non-native English speakers—integrate these tools into learning, or where AI fails to address accessibility barriers. This paper presents an eight-week autoethnographic study of a blind, Chinese-speaking doctoral student learning introductory Python through Khan Academy’s curriculum with screen readers, a Braille display, and AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini). Drawing on detailed learning diaries and human–AI interaction logs analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis, we examine how AI mediates accessibility, cognition, and language during programming learning. Findings show that AI simultaneously functions as an accessibility interpreter, cognitive scaffold, and linguistic mediator, yet also introduces epistemic uncertainty, accessibility hallucinations, inconsistent cross-lingual terminology, and clear limits with non-textual cues. We argue that AI reconfigures rather than solves accessibility, and derive design implications for AI-assisted programming tools prioritizing explicit code structure, screen-reader integration, calibrated trust, and terminology-aware multilingual support.

item.title: Balancing Safety and Autonomy: Accessibility-Oriented Interventions in Generative AI for Cognitive Impairment
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Generative AI systems are increasingly used by older adults with cognitive impairment for everyday tasks such as information seeking, health management, and communication. While these systems provide flexible, language-based support, their open-ended outputs introduce risks of over-reliance, misinterpretation, and inappropriate decision-making. Prior work has focused on usability and adoption, with limited attention to how system design shapes users’ participation in decision-making and the distribution of agency in care contexts. We present a qualitative study of 45 individuals with cognitive impairment and their caregivers. We identify five accessibility-oriented mechanisms: AI Capability Constraint, Human Oversight Embedding, Cognitive Engagement Maintenance, Human–AI Relationship Regulation, and Risk Transparency and Control, through which systems structure interaction. These mechanisms both support and constrain users by redistributing decision-making across users and caregivers. We show that their effects vary by impairment level: while protective mechanisms support users with severe impairment, they can restrict autonomy for those with mild impairment. As impairment progresses, tensions become less visible as user participation diminishes. Our findings highlight the need for dynamic designs that balance safety and autonomy in AI-supported care.

item.title: Towards Accessible AI Literacy: Investigating How Teachers of Blind and Low-Vision Students Integrate Generative AI in Pedagogical Practices
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools are reshaping the educational landscape; yet, how teachers working with blind and low vision (BLV) students integrate these tools into their pedagogical practices remains underexplored. To address this gap, we interviewed 17 teachers of BLV students to investigate how they leverage GenAI to fulfill their teaching responsibilities and educate BLV students about these tools. We found that teachers incorporated GenAI for personalized lesson planning and tasks specific to BLV education, while counteracting biases favoring sighted teaching methods. They addressed BLV students’ curiosity and concerns about GenAI and taught them prompt formulation strategies that support their access needs in academic and daily tasks, although occasionally perpetuating their own misconceptions about GenAI to students. They expressed concerns about students’ overreliance on GenAI lowering foundational accessibility-related skills. We discuss ways to promote accessible AI literacy and outline design considerations for incorporating GenAI to support teachers’ BLV-specific instructional responsibilities and for integrating GenAI responsibly in BLV education.

item.title: Supporting Allyship in Virtual Collaboration with Artificial Intelligence: A Scenario-Based Study
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Recent research has revealed that accessibility in virtual collaboration is not only a technical problem but also depends on allyship: the informal, interpersonal practices through which people support others’ accessibility needs. Yet little research has examined how artificial intelligence (AI) might support allyship in collaborative accessibility contexts. To address this gap, we conducted a study where 18 participants (10 disabled, 8 non-disabled) reflected on four allyship scenarios with novel AI tools. Participants valued AI designs that they anticipated could help teammates express, interpret, and coordinate around access needs by reducing repeated disclosure and making allyship more actionable. At the same time, participants raised concerns when AI acted without consent, misrepresented users’ intentions, or displaced the interpersonal work of allyship. Based on our findings, we introduce allyship-support tools as a class of accessibility technologies, offer design guidelines, and discuss AI in particular as a means of supporting allyship.

item.title: Human or Algorithmic Managers in Expert Knowledge Work? The Interplay of Management Style and Managerial Function
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Algorithmic management is entering expert knowledge work, but when workers accept algorithmic rather than human managers remains unclear. We surveyed Finnish expert knowledge workers (N = 1,156) using a factorial scenario experiment varying manager type (human/algorithmic), management style (controlling/balanced /flexible), and six managerial functions and measured leader–member exchange (LMX), organizational trust, AI familiarity and work complexity. Findings cover five functions; rewarding was excluded due to insufficient model fit. Management style was the strongest predictor: flexible styles were rated highest and controlling lowest, regardless of manager type. Human managers were preferred for goal setting, performance evaluation, and supportive leadership; algorithms only for scheduling under controlling conditions. Monitoring showed no consistent difference. High-quality LMX buffered reactions to controlling styles, and in performance evaluation and supportive leadership its association with acceptability was stronger for algorithmic managers, narrowing the human advantage. Organizational trust and LMX were more consistently implicated than AI familiarity, qualifying algorithm-aversion accounts.

item.title: How Large Language Models Weight Narrative Cues When Detecting Deception in Oral Accounts: A Multi‐Model Comparison
item.description:
Applied Cognitive Psychology
ABSTRACT Lie detection research has increasingly turned to artificial intelligence, yet the application of large language models (LLMs) remains underexplored for transcribed oral narratives. We compared five LLMs (Gemini‐3‐flash, Gemini‐3‐pro, Deepseek‐v4‐flash, GPT‐5.6‐luna, and Grok‐4) in classifying truthful and deceptive statements from interview transcripts of oral travel narratives collected from 95 Chinese‐speaking participants. Guided by Criteria‐Based Content Analysis (CBCA), Reality Monitoring (RM), and the Verifiability Approach (VA), theory‐driven prompts instructed models to score five narrative cues before making binary veracity judgments. Gemini‐3‐flash achieved the highest accuracy (74.74%, AUC = 0.76) with 81.63% sensitivity and 67.39% specificity, and stable repeated‐run performance. For this optimal model, unusual/superfluous details served as the sole significant predictor of objective veracity even after controlling for text length. LLMs can detect deception above chance but show large performance heterogeneity. Independent human coding, cross‐cultural replications, and adversarial robustness testing are needed before real‐world deployment.

item.title: Effects of question-chain prompting on self-regulated learning, metacognition, and achievement in a generative AI environment
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers learners immediate and personalized support, yet unguided interaction may encourage passive use and weaken self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether question-chain prompting can support SRL in human-AI interaction. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 83 undergraduates enrolled in a television program production course. A control group used free-form questioning, whereas two experimental groups used either a progressive or a divergent question-chain strategy. Data included GenAI interaction logs, post-task reflections, metacognitive awareness measures, and course grades. This study found that both question-chain groups demonstrated significantly more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. Reflection data further indicated differences in students’ approaches to human-AI collaboration, although these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the reflection prompts differed by condition. Moreover, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition, and academic achievement. No significant differences were found between the progressive and divergent question-chain approaches. The findings suggest that question-chain prompting, implemented as an instructional package of specific, sequenced, and required questions, can promote more active engagement during human-AI interaction and support metacognitive development and learning performance. Question chains offer a practical approach for guiding students’ use of GenAI in educational settings.

item.title: Gendered affective representations in AI-assisted music videos: a qualitative multimethod study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly visible in music-video production, influencing both production practices and the ways in which emotion, bodies, and gender are portrayed visually. This study examines gendered emotional representation in AI-assisted music videos. Methods A qualitative multimethod design combined interpretive visual analysis of four purposively selected AI-assisted music videos with asynchronous written expert interviews involving six creative-industry professionals and four psychology experts ( N = 10). The videos were analysed through an interpretive coding framework covering emotion, gender, body and face, power relations, AI aesthetics, and traces of bias. Results Across the cases, emotion was conveyed not only through facial expression but also through atmosphere, colour, movement, editing, and spatial transitions. The selected works sometimes reproduced familiar conventions, including heteronormative intimacy, militarised masculinity, and idealised female bodies, but also unsettled them through female anger and solidarity and mutable synthetic bodies. Ambiguity in a body’s appearance did not necessarily unsettle its gendered narrative role. Industry accounts described how prompting, selection, revision, and post-production shape representations, while general psychology-expert perspectives informed their interpretation. Discussion The findings position AI-assisted music videos as co-produced sites of synthetic visual culture in which established gendered conventions may be repeated, negotiated, or challenged. Neither expert group provided direct evidence about the production or reception of the selected videos. The findings underline the practical importance of representational review, consent, diversity, and transparent disclosure in AI-assisted cultural production.

item.title: How AI disclosure influences consumers' purchase intention toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion: the roles of perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background With the growing application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in fashion design and cultural and creative industries, AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion has created new opportunities for the contemporary transformation of traditional culture. However, whether consumers are willing to accept such products and how AI disclosure influences their evaluations and purchase intentions remain unclear. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model, this study examines the mechanisms through which AI disclosure, design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion influence consumers' purchase intentions toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion. Methods A questionnaire survey combined with a scenario-based experiment was employed. Six AI-generated fashion illustrations derived from Tujia costume elements were developed and selected as stimulus materials. Participants were randomly assigned to either an AI disclosure group or a non-disclosure group. Data were collected through Tencent Questionnaire, yielding 410 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) were employed to examine the structural relationships, mediating effects, moderating effects, and practical priorities for improvement. Results Design aesthetics and cultural identity influenced purchase intention through perceived usefulness and perceived authenticity, with perceived usefulness emerging as the strongest predictor of purchase intention. AI disclosure significantly reduced design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, and perceived authenticity. Algorithm aversion did not significantly moderate the relationship between perceived usefulness and purchase intention but significantly strengthened the positive effect of perceived authenticity on purchase intention. Conclusions This study reveals the multiple psychological pathways through which AI disclosure shapes consumers' evaluations of AI-generated ethnic cultural fashion. The findings further indicate that algorithm aversion alters the extent to which consumers rely on authenticity judgments when forming purchase intentions. This study extends the application of the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model to the context of AI-generated cultural products and provides practical implications for balancing AI transparency, cultural authenticity, and the practical value of products.

item.title: AI Tutors in Technical Training: Trust, Feedback Timing, and Skill Transfer in Maintenance Tasks
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Technical maintenance training requires learners to develop procedural accuracy, diagnostic reasoning, error recovery, and confidence under realistic conditions. This study examined how AI tutor feedback timing influences trust, over-reliance, and skill transfer in maintenance tasks. Participants completed procedures under three conditions: immediate feedback, delayed feedback, and adaptive feedback triggered by hesitation, repeated errors, or safety-critical risk. Outcomes included training accuracy, recovery quality, completion time, cognitive workload, tutor trust, feedback acceptance, and unaided transfer performance. Immediate feedback improved early accuracy and reduced procedural errors but increased step-by-step dependence and weakened independent troubleshooting. Delayed feedback produced mixed effects, supporting autonomy for some learners while increasing frustration and avoidable mistakes for others. Adaptive feedback produced the strongest results by allowing independent attempts while intervening when support was needed. It improved unaided transfer, error recovery, procedural sequencing, and trust calibration. Overall, AI tutors were most effective when feedback scaffolded learning without replacing trainee judgment.

item.title: Do You Feel Like Using GenAI? Scenario Emotional Valence Impact on Potential Generative Artificial Intelligence Use
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) is becoming increasingly ubiquitous, creating questions about what factors are influencing its use. This study explored whether emotions in decision-making scenarios impact the use of genAI writing tools. We presented 35 writing-based scenarios, some associated with the six basic human emotions (sadness, anger, enjoyment, fear, surprise, disgust) and others created as neutral emotional conditions. College student participants were asked whether they would use a genAI tool to complete the task, and then to identify the emotion present. Most participants varied their decision to use AI tools. There were significant effects of emotion on the potential use of genAI assistance, with a higher intended adoption for fear and surprise contexts. Emotion strength also influenced potential AI use, with reported AI trust and task complexity increasing in stronger-rated scenarios. However, the overall rate of AI use was generally low. Implications for automation use and trust theories are discussed.

item.title: When AI Enters the Pencil Box: A Longitudinal Study of Child–LLM Writing Collaboration in a Chinese Primary School
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
We report a qualitative study spanning more than six months with upper-primary students (ages 9–12) in southern China using a local LLM (Doubao) for writing. Two interview waves with ten students (nine re-interviewed) and six teachers (three re-interviewed) reveal a set of recurring shifts in our focal cohort: from novelty to strategy, from anthropomorphic “companion/virtual teacher” to tool-like framing, and from quick unsticking to guarded use shaped by dependence, fairness, and exam-transfer Footnote1 concerns. Students valued speed and breadth but noted mechanical tone, age/style mismatch, and weak transfer to AI-free tests. We map a Control × Dependency framework and before/after transitions, and surface tensions around classroom norms and equity amid policy ambiguity and uneven AI literacy. We suggest process-visible, agency-preserving integration: sentence- and phrase-level provenance with mandatory micro-edits, task-specific scaffold ceilingsFootnote2, and process-anchored assessment schemes that explicitly factor in AI-use traces.

item.title: Does Code-Switching Disrupt Emotion Recognition? A Valence–Arousal Analysis of Affective Misalignment in Multilingual Human–AI Interaction
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
As multilingual communication increasingly involves code-switching, emotion recognition in mixed-language input has become a key challenge for human–AI interaction. This study examines emotion classification under English–Spanish and Spanish–English code-switching conditions using the valence–arousal framework. Five large language models (GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-5, Llama-3, Llama-4, and Claude Opus 4.7) were evaluated on 7,560 inputs across five code-switching ratios. Performance was assessed using accuracy, Macro-F1, and mixed-effects logistic regression, while errors were categorized as valence shifts, arousal shifts, or same-region confusions. Increasing code-switching produced a small but significant accuracy decline in both language directions. Under English-to-Spanish conditions, models generally preserved valence while showing greater arousal instability. Under Spanish-to-English conditions, GPT-5 showed increased valence-shift errors and was the only model with a significant direction–error-type association. Aggregate metrics can obscure distinct forms of affective misalignment. The proposed framework enables dimension-level comparison of error patterns across models, language directions, and code-switching ratios.

item.title: From AI labels to trust: cognitive pathways linking authenticity judgments, risk perception, and trust in AI-generated videos
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) has raised concerns regarding the authenticity and trustworthiness of synthetic media. Although AI disclosure labels are increasingly used as transparency mechanisms, the cognitive processes through which these cues influence trust formation remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to develop and test a cognitive pathway model explaining how AI disclosure labels, authenticity judgments, perceived risk, cognitive processing styles, and literacy factors shape trust toward AI-generated videos. Methods A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 617 participants randomly assigned to four conditions involving AI-generated instructional videos with different AI label and video quality combinations. Participants evaluated authenticity, systematic and heuristic processing, trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, sharing intention, AI literacy, and media literacy. Regression, bootstrapped mediation, and moderation analyses were performed. Results AI disclosure labels significantly reduced perceived authenticity but did not directly affect trust, adoption, sharing intention, or perceived risk. Trust formation occurred through cognitive pathways: systematic processing increased trust, whereas heuristic processing reduced trust. Authenticity enhanced trust and lowered perceived risk, with perceived risk mediating the authenticity–trust relationship. Trust positively predicted adoption and sharing intentions, while AI and media literacy moderated selected relationships. Conclusion Trust in AI-generated videos was not directly determined by transparency labels alone. Instead, the observed associations among authenticity judgments, perceived risk, information processing, and trust were consistent with a multi-stage cognitive interpretation, although the cross-sectional post-exposure measurement of these constructs does not establish their temporal or causal sequence.

item.title: Monitoring AI-generated English research texts: lexical-semantic accuracy, source fidelity, and revision performance
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Linguistically fluent AI-generated English texts can conceal lexical-semantic shifts, altered concept boundaries, source omissions, and unsupported causal formulations. This study compared English paragraphs generated under general and source-constrained conditions and examined how learners' global judgments and localized problem marking were associated with subsequent written revision. Methods Seventy-three agricultural and forestry students evaluated two English paragraphs generated from Chinese source materials under a fixed sequence of general and source-constrained prompts, then selected and revised one paragraph. The linked corpus comprised 146 AI-generated texts, 73 revised texts, 146 global judgment records, 657 expert rating records, 562 coded terminology units, and 511 participant-marked problems. Expert assessments covered lexical-semantic accuracy, source fidelity, and global discourse organization, while revision analyses examined global judgment discrepancy, localized problem marking, and individual-difference variables. Results Source-constrained texts received higher lexical-semantic accuracy scores (mean difference = 0.846, t = 10.634, p < 0.001, d z = 1.245) and source-fidelity scores (mean difference = 0.855, t = 8.819, p < 0.001, d z = 1.032), while global discourse organization differed little between conditions. Lexical-semantic accuracy was strongly associated with source fidelity ( b = 0.522, p < 0.001), whereas the 5,000-resample bootstrap interval for the product of the adjusted coefficients linking these measures to discourse organization spanned zero. After controlling for selected source-text quality, localized problem marking and domain knowledge were positively associated with revised quality, trust in AI-generated language output was negatively associated, and global judgment discrepancy showed no unique association. Discussion Source comparison and localized problem identification were more closely associated with successful written revision than agreement with expert global judgments. These findings highlight the importance of attending to linguistic form, semantic boundaries, and source information when evaluating and revising AI-generated English research texts.

item.title: “I Just Needed Someone to Listen”: A Community Discussion Analysis of Redditors’ Discourse About Using General-Purpose LLMs for Therapy
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Despite increasing efforts of legislatures to prohibit specialized AI-driven apps from providing therapeutic decision-making, general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as alternative tools for mental health support. In this paper, we examine the increased adoption of AI for mental health through the lens of proponents’ and opponents’ discussions on public forums. Through a qualitative analysis of 67 Reddit discussion threads (totaling 2948 comments), we offer an in-depth investigation of the various contexts in which users rely on (or fail to rely on) AI for mental health support, as well as an analysis of the main discussions (including positions for and against the use of AI for therapy) within the community. By critically reflecting on our findings, we highlight ethical considerations and discuss how research, design and regulation of AI tools can help improve mental health support for users with complicated needs while mitigating potential harms.

item.title: Negotiating agency: university students’ experiences of co-creating content with generative AI
item.description:
Education and Information Technologies

item.title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
item.description:
British Journal of Educational Technology
Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. Implications for practice and/or policy Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems. Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning. We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.

item.title: A study of the impact of AI-employee collaboration on employee innovation behavior
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction With the deep integration of digitalization and generative artificial intelligence, artificial intelligence has transformed from a mere technical tool into a core collaborative partner within modern workplaces and human‑resource management. As an interdependent human‑AI working mode characterized by complementary task division, joint task accomplishment, complementary decision‑making, and continuous iterative interaction between employees and AI agents, AI‑employee collaboration is conceptually distinct from simple AI adoption, instrumental AI use, and AI‑assisted technical systems. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the present study aims to investigate how AI‑employee collaboration predicts employee innovation behavior, alongside the mediating role of self‑efficacy and the moderated‑mediation boundary condition of servant leadership. Methods Three‑wave time‑lagged questionnaire data were collected from 259 employees working in internet‑service, finance, and catering industries across Beijing and Jinan. Hierarchical regression and bootstrap approaches were adopted to test the proposed moderated‑mediation model. Results The results show that AI‑employee collaboration exerts a significant positive predictive effect on employee innovation behavior. Self‑efficacy partially mediates the relationship between AI‑employee collaboration and employee innovation behavior. Moreover, servant leadership positively moderates the link between AI‑employee collaboration and self‑efficacy and further strengthens the indirect predictive effect of AI‑employee collaboration on employee innovation behavior through self‑efficacy. Discussion This research enriches existing literature by providing incremental empirical evidence for the internal cognitive mechanism and contextual boundary of AI‑driven employee innovation. Theoretically, it unpacks the cognitive “black box” connecting AI‑employee collaboration and employee innovation and identifies servant leadership as a key situational contingency factor. Practically, these findings deliver concrete, actionable managerial insights for digitally transforming organizations to leverage AI tools and unlock employees’ innovative potential.

item.title: Integrating Generative AI Into an Undergraduate Research Methods Course: Evaluating Student Perceptions, AI Competency, and Intention to Use
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
College students increasingly use generative AI, yet formal undergraduate classroom implementation remains limited. This study evaluated a structured generative AI training in an undergraduate research methods course, examining its impact on students’ perceptions, self-rated competency, and future intention to use. Early in the semester, students received a lecture on generative AI tools, applications, and ethical issues, including bias, plagiarism, and data privacy. Two optional assignments provided hands-on practice using AI for literature searching and academic writing. After the course, 24 of 195 enrolled students completed a survey. Respondents reported low-to-moderate initial AI familiarity and competency. The lecture was well received and led to confidence in citing and disclosing AI use. Students expressed moderately positive intentions to use AI for future studying and research activities, while reporting concerns about accuracy and academic integrity. Findings suggest that structured, evidence-based AI training may support responsible use in undergraduates while addressing persistent ethical and practical concerns.

item.title: Exploring foreign language learners' GenAI-coexisted peer argumentation
item.description:
Learning Culture and Social Interaction
